title: The Hanuman Chalisa
hookLine: the hymn many Hindus know by heart begins with a mirror and ends at Ram's door
carry: dasya: Hanuman's strength is for serving Ram
tomorrow: why did a teacher tell a singer to stop whining?

cards: A truck driver in traffic, murmuring under his breath. A student outside an exam hall, lips moving. A grandmother on a Tuesday evening, a small book open on her lap that she doesn't need, because she knows every word.
They could all be saying the same thing: a hymn to Hanuman, short enough to say in a few minutes, steady enough to lean on. Tradition gives it to Tulsidas, and the hymn signs his name near its end.

teach.h: POLISH THE MIRROR OF THE MIND.
teach.b: The Hanuman Chalisa doesn't start with Hanuman. It starts with a mirror. The first couplet says, roughly: with the dust from my teacher's lotus feet I polish the mirror of my mind, and then I sing the pure fame of Ram.
Before praising anyone, clean the glass, so what you see isn't smudged by you. The second couplet is even more honest.
Knowing myself to be without understanding, it says, I remember Hanuman, son of the wind. Give me strength, wisdom and knowledge, and take away my troubles. That's the posture of the whole hymn.

Not I am strong, but I'm not wise enough, so I'm calling on the one who is. Then the verses praise Hanuman piece by piece: his strength, his leap across the sea, the healing herb that revived Lakshman.
But one line says what all that strength is for.
Hanuman is the guard at Ram's door. All that power, used for service, near Ram, doing what's needed. Near the end, the poet steps forward with his own name.
Tulsidas, the hymn says, is forever Hari's servant, and he asks the Lord to make a home in his heart. So the poet ends where Hanuman stands: a servant.
Bhakti has a name for this love: dasya, the love of a servant for the Lord, and Hanuman is its great example.

It's why many Hindus say the Chalisa before an exam, a journey, a hard night: not as a lucky charm, but to clean the mirror, ask for strength, wisdom and knowledge, and use them the way Hanuman did, for someone else.

how: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often from memory, at home and in temples, and some make a point of saying it on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

games.q: you're about to sing a hymn of praise to Hanuman. what does the Chalisa do first?
o: polish the mirror of the mind with the teacher's foot-dust.
games.why: it starts with a mirror: clean the mind with the dust of the teacher's feet, then sing. then it admits it lacks understanding.

practice: Picture your mind as a glass with the day's smudges on it, a worry, a grudge, a hurry, and with each breath out, let one smudge soften.

Then, if it feels honest, admit one thing you don't understand right now, and ask quietly for the strength to serve anyway. If you pray, you can turn that asking to God, or to Hanuman, in whatever words you already use.
